inputs.source: Chat question from an SSO-authenticated employee
Engineering design docs, write-restricted to engineers
Jira tickets filed by customers (planned MCP connection, next sprint)

instructions.note: The sole safeguard against leaking secrets or credentials is a prompt instruction (behavioral, dependent); no structural output filter exists, and this gap becomes more consequential once an egress-capable tool is added.

controls.name: Prompt instruction forbidding secrets or credentials in answers
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model choosing to comply; a goal-hijacked or more capable model can rationalize exceptions or split forbidden content across steps, especially once ticket-sourced untrusted content can drive tool calls.

controls.name: Read-only credential scoping docs.search
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by credential scope outside the model; does not weaken as the model becomes more capable, and only widens if the design deliberately expands the grant (data_scope_expansion).

controls.name: Replies restricted to the authenticated requester; no link or image rendering in the chat client
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the chat client and session binding rather than by model choice. It is defeated only if a new output channel is added, for example link rendering, image rendering, or a new egress tool.

controls.name: Egress allowlist restricting web.fetch destinations
controls.decay_rationale: Would be enforced outside the model at the network layer; recommended for when web.fetch is built. Does not yet exist.

controls.name: Provenance tagging marking Jira ticket content as untrusted
controls.decay_rationale: Would spotlight ticket content as data rather than instructions; a sufficiently adaptive injection can still partially defeat it, so it is only partially dependent rather than independent.

controls.name: Output filter blocking confidential content encoded in web.fetch arguments
controls.decay_rationale: A separate classifier on tool-call arguments decays more slowly than the model itself, but encoding or paraphrase can still get past it.

controls.name: Human approval gate on web.fetch calls influenced by untrusted content
controls.decay_rationale: Recommended as a raw-action, low-volume gate; does not yet exist because the tool is not yet built.

controls.name: Tamper-evident audit log of docs_search queries and replies
controls.decay_rationale: Recommended logging enforced outside the model; does not exist today.

controls.name: Rate limit or spend cap on web.fetch
controls.decay_rationale: Recommended cap enforced outside the model; does not exist because the tool is not yet built.

findings.title: No attributable record of agent actions, and no rate or spend limit on tool use

forecast.watch_signal: web.fetch entering the tool manifest or the Jira server entering the MCP client config without an accompanying audit log or rate/spend limit shipped alongside it.

evidence.observation: No logging, audit trail, rate limit, or spend cap is described for docs.search or chat replies.
The roadmap adds web.fetch, a capability with real external cost and abuse potential, with no mention of limits or logging.

recommendations.action: Add a tamper-evident audit log recording each docs_search query, requester identity, and (once added) each web.fetch destination, so actions are attributable.
Add a rate limit or spend cap on web.fetch before enabling it, since it will be the agent's first capability with real-world cost and abuse potential.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): planned Jira tickets plus confidential docs read plus web.fetch egress

attack_path.note: Customer-filed ticket content enters the agent's context once the planned Jira MCP connection is added; untrusted source.
Agent searches confidential engineering design docs in response to a ticket-driven goal.
Agent calls the planned web.fetch tool with a URL that can encode the retrieved confidential content, exfiltrating it to an external destination.

threat_refs.name: Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

forecast.watch_signal: web.fetch appearing in the tool manifest or MCP tools/list response, and a Jira server entry appearing in the MCP client config.

evidence.observation: Next sprint adds a web.fetch tool for public references and a Jira MCP server that includes tickets filed by customers.
Design docs are confidential and are the only data docs.search can read; no egress capability or untrusted input currently reaches it.

The only control that would apply to the new sink is a behavioral prompt instruction not to paste secrets or credentials, which does not address exfiltration of ordinary confidential content via a crafted URL.

recommendations.action: Before enabling web.fetch, add an egress allowlist restricting destinations to a small set of vetted public documentation domains and block free-form query parameters that could carry confidential content.
When the Jira connector is added, tag customer-filed ticket content as untrusted and spotlight it so it is never treated as an instruction to the agent.
Require raw-action, low-volume human approval for any web.fetch call whose arguments were influenced by ticket content.

stride_coverage.rationale: The agent is a first-party internal service with no external peer connections today, so there is no external peer identity to spoof.
The artifacts do not describe how the docs.search tool definition is maintained, versioned, or protected from modification.
The agent performs at most one docs.search call per request with no looping, delegation, or spend capability, so a runaway resource-consumption loop is not reachable in this design.
The store is read-only from the agent's perspective and at most one search call occurs per request, so sustained exhaustion of the store is not reachable from this design.
Peer identity verification for the planned Jira MCP server has not been specified in the roadmap note.
Whether tool or server definitions from the planned Jira connection will be pinned or hashed is not yet specified.
Audit logging for the planned Jira connector has not been described in the available artifacts.
Rate limiting or quota design for the planned Jira connector is not yet specified in the roadmap note.
Credential scope for the planned Jira integration, including whether it uses a shared service account, is not yet specified.
Volume limits or throttling for ingesting customer-filed tickets have not been specified in the roadmap note.
Whether customer identity is verified when a ticket is filed, through an authenticated portal or open submission, is not specified.
Attribution of ticket content to a specific customer account for accountability has not been described.
Authentication for destinations that web.fetch calls, if any, is not specified in the roadmap note.
Whether the web.fetch tool definition or destination list will be pinned or hashed is not yet specified.
Credential scope for web.fetch, including whether it can reach internal network ranges, has not been specified.

rating.rationale: Today docs-qa is a read-only, internal Q&A agent: the only sensitive data it can read (confidential design docs) has no reachable egress path, replies go only to the authenticated requester, and the chat client renders no links or images, so inherent and residual risk are both low. The roadmap plans to add two things in the same sprint: a web.fetch tool (the agent's first egress-capable capability) and a Jira MCP connection that ingests tickets filed by customers (the agent's first untrusted input). Together these complete a lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted ticket content could direct the agent to read confidential docs and encode them into a web.fetch request. The only control that would nominally cover that path is a behavioral prompt instruction not to paste secrets, which does not address ordinary confidential content and decays further under model upgrades. No egress allowlist, input provenance tagging, approval gate, audit log, or rate limit is described for either planned addition, so the forecast rises to high.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.
No MCP configuration, IaC, or tool manifest was provided; capability scope is inferred from the system prompt and a short roadmap note, so confidence is medium at best.

Implementation details of the planned web.fetch tool and Jira MCP connection (authentication, destination scope, rate limits, audit logging) are not yet specified; the forecast finding makes conservative assumptions about typical implementations of such features and should be re-run once those details are known.
